summary:
Allwork.Space profiles SAP CEO Christian Klein, interviewed at the World Economic Forum in Davos, who predicts the keyboard's decline as a business data-input device. Klein argues voice recognition built on large language models is now strong enough that typing data into SAP systems will end at the firm within two to three years, though work remains to translate voice into business language and business data. Users will instead ask analytical questions aloud, trigger operational task workflows, and make entries such as performance feedback and pipeline records by voice. The piece frames 2026 as the era of applied rather than theoretical AI, with software vendors generating substantial revenue.

Klein divides companies into two AI adoption camps: those saying AI is changing how they run the business, and those who spent heavily but see low value. He attributes failure to treating AI as an efficiency hack confined to one division or function, with no reach across the rest of the firm. He advocates applying AI horizontally across the whole business, with employee training. An example: a large consumer goods client where an agent predicts demand better than its human planners, but inventory adjustment still took months because of procurement and manufacturing dependencies. SAP is building an end-to-end agentic planning scenario projected to optimize inventory by 20%.

Another example describes employees feeding millions of financial analysis PowerPoints to an AI model to surface recommended measures, packaged with graphs, commentary and recommended actions.

The article closes on geopolitics: Trump's Greenland annexation threat and tariff wars dominated Davos, spheres of influence and mercantilism are returning, and the G4 (America, China, Europe, India) diverge on trade. Klein cites rising sovereignty requirements, including in-country cloud servers and differing data protection rules, forcing global software vendors to adapt to a fragmented world.

Background: SAP stands for Systemanalyse Programmentwicklung, was founded in 1972 and is headquartered in Walldorf, Germany.

claims.claim: English engineer Henry Mill submitted the first patent for a machine transcribing letters in 1714, a forerunner of the typewriter and electronic keyboard, though it never went into production
